utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, honourable gentlemen, good morning. Yes, I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Wubben. And good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned colleagues from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones, I represent the defence for Mr. Naser Oric. We have our legal assistant here, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries? No? Yesterday we finished on a note arising in the wake of some comments that were made by Ms. Sellers. I couldn't exactly understand whether it was an objection or not. But anyway, I consider the matter raised by Ms. Sellers as extremely relevant, and I don't think I need to -- I would be offending you if I did. I don't think I need to explain what the purpose, what the nature of cross-examination are. What concerns me and what worries me, and this happens in every case, not just in this case, is that there is a temptation sometimes, and a strong temptation, which I have a feeling that Defence lawyers, in particular, are very happy to succumb to, of taking advantage of the presence of a witness here to expose, in as bad a light as possible, the other side, so to say, not the Prosecution but the other ethnic group. If it is a Serbian that is -- if it is a Serb that is being accused, then the tendency is to forget that he is the accused and the cannons are turned on the other ethnic groups. It is natural, I mean, it's something that is to be expected, because, after all, we're talking of a conflict that took place and its events are relatively still recent, and sometimes there is some validity also in the fact -- in the facts that are attached to the other side involved in the conflict. However, Ms. Vidovic, in particular, I should like to remind you that who is accused in this trial is not Slobodan Milosevic, it's not Karadzic, it's not the government of Republika Srpska, it's not the government of Serbia or Montenegro. Certainly not, it's not the Serbian people. Certainly not, it's not the Serbian people. Who is accused in this trial is your client. So I do understand you trying to bring out some of the events particular to the conflict and that occurred before, and sometimes even after the conflict, because I do understand that sometimes some events are definitely relevant. But on the other hand, I mean, what is more relevant is the events that are particularly the substance of the indictment and of which -- and which form the basis of the charges that your client has to answer. So I don't know, this is in addition, over and above what Ms. Sellers pointed out yesterday. For example, I mean, I don't know, but the purpose of cross-examination is to bring out, in perspective in particular, anything that you contest to the witness. I mean, your client is a military officer, high-ranking military officer. I mean, I haven't heard any questions on, for example, the command structure -- as far as the command structure -- on the Serbian side, yes, I have heard. But I haven't heard anything on the military structure on the Muslim side, for example. I'm mentioning these because we've discussed a little bit amongst ourselves, and we are a little bit concerned that so far, we have been having sort of a cross-examination at a tangent. Rather than a direct cross-examination to the core issues, we have a cross-examination to try and bring out whatever is bad, in your view, in the conflict and which could be attributed to the other side. In actual fact, it's not the other side that's being tried here in this trial. It may be tried in other trials, but not in this trial. So I appeal to you to go straight to the core issues and limit your cross-examination to what a cross-examination ought to be. With that, I think we can admit the witness and we can proceed. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, I wonder if we might at least respond to the points raised by Ms. Sellers and the points raised by Your Honours, because indeed Rule 90(H)(i) goes beyond the parameters what Your Honour has said. I leave that to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will first try to briefly respond to what Ms. Patricia Sellers said, and then I will also try to explain -- to give an explanation in relation to your comments here. Yesterday in her objection, the Prosecutor said that we presented evidence that in no way opposed the thesis put forth by Mr. Gow, and that the Defence should use Mr. Gow to cross-examine him in relation to the facts that the Defence disagrees with. Your Honour, I refer your attention to Rule 90(H)(i) that we all know, that the restriction in a cross-examination and the credibility of the witness examined, but it does allow the questioning side, in this case the Defence, that the witness who can give favourable statements for the Defence should, therefore, ask these questions. And this is the case here. Chapter 3, the military and political context of this case contained in his report, clearly indicates the relevancy of our case that I made clear in my cross-examination yesterday. The Rules are -- do not provide for a situation where the questioning -- the cross-examining side should be obliged to put only those questions that relate to the matters that the questioning side disagrees with. Quite the contrary. As is the case with Dr. Gow, quite the contrary. In the case of Dr. Gow, I am here referring to the requests by the Prosecutor to admit Dr. Gow's report in accordance with Rule 94 bis of 13 September 2004. We were willing to cross-examine him, not to criticise his qualifications, competence, or relevance of any part of his report. Quite the contrary. We insisted on having him here as a witness because we intended to examine this witness, who knows facts that are very relevant to our case, in order for him to explain the entire context of the conflict and the background of the conflict. This is, in our submission, of 2nd October 2004. With all due respect, I think that my cross-examination of yesterday was fully in compliance with this rule. Ms. Sellers also pointed out the issue of facts in dispute. We are very careful in examining what we are going to stipulate to and what we are not going to stipulate to in the interests of our client. As for the background of the case, we accepted 26 out of 30 facts that the Prosecutor delivered to us in a letter dated 30 September, that was enclosed with the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. The facts under 5, 6, and 7 contained in that letter relate to the remainder of the cadre of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina and its preparation for the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as to the functioning of the Territorial Defence under the control of the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, under the control of the Muslims. Yesterday the Prosecutor, on page 97, lines 11 to 15, asked that we stipulate to the fact that, after the breakup of Yugoslavia, the remainder of the JNA officers started preparing the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We asked no such thing of Dr. Gow yesterday. We do not think that it's true, in fact, and that is our case. As for item 30 that was offered to us and that was raised again yesterday by Ms. Sellers, the fact that was proposed to be stipulated to, that was on the page of the transcript number 97, lines 18 to 20, that the JNA had provided the key military, financial and logistics assistance to the VRS forces. As for that, we wanted to have Dr. Gow's explanation as to what it was all about. His explanation given on page 80 of the transcript, line 25, and page 81 and line 1, is drastically different to the position of the Prosecutor as contained in their offer for stipulation. I will also briefly turn to what Your Honour has said. I would kindly ask you to understand that the existence of an international conflict for our case, for the case of our client, is not of essential importance. It is crucially important for us to determine the presence of the military forces on the ground, meaning on the ground in those municipalities that are mentioned together with the allegations against our client, regardless of whether these are Yugoslav, Montenegrin, or local Serb units. It is very relevant for us to establish and prove that there was a presence of very strong military units on the ground, of heavy weaponry, aircraft, military structures, all those elements that would come under the military necessity. And that is the reason why my examination of Dr. Gow was a very detailed one. The issues of the command structure within the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, specifically when it comes to our client, are of a very peculiar nature. You will have occasion to see during the case that there was almost no such structure there at all. Secondly, Dr. Gow said at one point yesterday that because the structure was cut off, he was not dealing with the structure as such at all, because the issue of the structure of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a peculiar issue, an issue that is actually aside from all the events that took place in Srebrenica. And I appeal to you to allow us to try and present the situation to the Chamber as it was, in fact, in Srebrenica, from the military perspective, everything that my client is charged with, and, of course, to present the situation as the fact that it was trying to wear out the refugees, allow them to starve, and all the other issues that definitely are relevant to our case. I apologise for having taken up quite a lot of your time, but these are the reasons why my questions were as they were yesterday. As for the facts to be stipulated, we have analysed carefully the proposal, the submissions put forth by the Prosecutor yesterday, and our position remains unchanged. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we have heard enough on this matter. Usher, could you please admit the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just ask for the record, prior to the witness coming in that we would like to respond to the Defence and your concerns. We certainly accept any decision that you take. We do renew -- they're looking at the stipulations, and under Rule 90(H)(ii), we don't believe that they are confronting the witness with contradiction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fine. I don't think I have been read well. The idea of having a cross-examination is to advance your position, and I hope the point is taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And sometimes I was even taught in my very first case as a lawyer in my country, that sometimes it's wiser to sit down and not even put a single question to a witness in cross-examination. Dr. Gow, good morning. My apologies to you for having kept you waiting for 25 minutes in that room, or perhaps even more. But we threshed the matter that we started discussing in your presence yesterday. Again, I'm just reminding you that you are testifying on the basis of a solemn declaration that you took two days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask the usher to show Dr. Gow a document by the Ministry of Defence. This is D55.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Gow, would you please look at this document. This is a document by the Ministry of Defence, sent to the governments of the autonomous regions and the SAO, delivers the decision by the Serbian Assembly, adopted on the 15th of March, 1992. Could you please look at Article 1 of the decision, which reads: "The Territorial Defence --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Madam Vidovic, could we have it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "The Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is hereby established as an armed force of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Territorial Defence -- the following will be in command and control of the Territorial Defence: Municipal district and regional staffs, and the republican staff of SBiHTO. The decision on other components of the armed forces will be adopted, pursuant to an agreement on the political setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the status of JNA. All the military conscripts shall place themselves at the disposal of the Serbian TO in the territory of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina." Mr. Gow, have your studies shown that the Territorial Defence 4, since its establishment, formed a component part of the army and was not a structure functioning outside the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was initially seen as a separate institution/organisation, but it was clear, which is also in line, I guess, with the old Yugoslav defence doctrine that it was intended at the time of operations to be integrated as a whole. It was the basis, or one of the bases, for forming what became the VRS. This document seems to be making clear the idea that the Territorial Defence will be subjugated and part of the army that is formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the Defence Exhibit D56 in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I point out, I didn't get the original version of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will quote: "The units so far and the staffs of the Territorial Defence --" this is a decision by the Assembly of the Serbian People on the establishment of the army of the Serbian Republic of 12 May 1992. "The units and staffs of the Territorial Defence, as they were so far, are transformed into commands and army units whose organisation and establishment will be determined by the president of the republic." Dr. Gow, is it not true that units and staffs of the Territorial Defence were merely renamed into commands and units of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, that they were merely renamed?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what this law says, yes, that of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And would it then be correct that all the armed forces were involved, all the Serb armed forces were involved in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not entirely clear what you mean by "all Serb armed forces," because it wasn't necessarily the case, for example, that paramilitary forces were involved in it, although they were clearly working with it on an operational basis. Technically, sometimes they were seen as independent. Sometimes, technically, they were formerly -- there was a law in Belgrade in December 1991 that nobody ever really noticed that subjugated them to the Belgrade authorities and it meant that they could be incorporated within the JNA as well. I've never seen such a law, but I half suspect that there was one applying to the VRS as well, which would say they would be subjugated to. But I don't think it makes a difference. I think in the end, what is clear, that is, that all of these Serbian forces were subject to the same ultimate authority within the same ultimate programme of activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that the TO, since the establishment of the army of Republika Srpska, was indeed part of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... the answer to the previous question as well, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Can I have the usher's assistance now. I would like to place the following document on the ELMO. It is a document of the Bratunac Brigade. The title is "To All Units," signed by the Commander Svetozar Andric. This document is an excerpt from the financial records of the Bratunac Brigade in relation to August 1992. I will quote from this document now. "By a telegramme dated the 13th of September, 26/9/43, dated the 13th of September, 1992, from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, we have been informed on the exact amounts for the salaries for the month of August." And then there is a list that follows, if you can please have a look, the specific amounts in relation to specific categories of officers and privates. I would like to ask you the following: Has your research perhaps shown that members of the army of Republika Srpska were, in fact, paid? Did it receive financial compensation for their participation in the armed struggle? And were there any records that were being kept of these payments, if any?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: My research indicates that a lot of the time people were not being paid, although they were supposed to be paid; that officers were being paid from a budget from the Federal Ministry of Defence in Belgrade. I can say this document seems to confirm what the pay rates would be at that particular time for members of the VRS. I don't know if -- if you're asking me to confirm what the document says or to talk about wider issues, but I think I've done both a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. Yesterday you said at one point that General Ratko Mladic was appointed as the new commander of the Main Staff. Therefore, Dr. Gow, can you please have a look at the following document, prior to which I would like to have this previous document assigned a number as a Defence exhibit, the document that we just used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The next number is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Defence Exhibit D74.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered and admitted in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D74. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document was signed by General Ratko Mladic. The title is "Directive of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska for the Month of August 1992." Can you please look at page 3, Dr. Gow. The title is "Operational Objectives." If you can please look at paragraph 4, the last sentence orders as follows: "Crush Ustasha forces in the Birac area." And on page 5, item 5.3, the East Bosnia Corps, the main East Bosnia Corps. I'm talking about page 5, item 5.3?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. It goes on to page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the two references Madam Vidovic has made, on the English -- in the English text, the reference is on -- the first reference is on page 01905851. It's under the section headed "Operations Objectives," fourth bulleted paragraph, three lines from the bottom of that paragraph, "crush Ustasha forces in the areas of Birac." The second reference is on page 5, on page 5 of the English text, with ERN number 01905853, and it's the third -- towards the top of the page. The paragraph is numbered 5.3 and starts with the words "Eastern Bosnia Corps." That's just for the record. You can, I suppose, follow from that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I might point out that I've now put the original reference, the one with "crush Ustasha" on here. I shall put the other in a moment. But can I point out that there appears to be an extraneous page with a completely different number in the middle here, which I think is what created a problem when if it -- when the issue's put on. If I can give this page to somebody to see where else it might belong. So we have page 3, for the record, in the English translation, which makes reference to "crush Ustasha forces in the area of Birac, Visegrad, Gorazde, Trnovo, and Foca." And I'll place the second quotation now. Can somebody remind me which point it was? It was page 5, yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 5, paragraph 5.3, at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: 5.3, "the East Bosnia Corps, the main forces in cooperation with the 1st Krajina Corps, free from the Ustasha forces, the areas of Majevica, Semberija, and Birac." Dr. Gow, you confirmed yesterday that Birac is an area including the municipalities of Bratunac, Srebrenica, Zvornik, and Vlasenica. Is it not correct, Dr. Gow, that since August 1991, there had been orders to crush the forces in the Birac area, to crush the Muslim forces specifically in the Birac area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document indicates to crush Ustasha forces in that area, which is a little curious, because you would usually assume Ustasha to refer to Croatian forces rather than to Muslim forces. So it's not clear to me what is being said here. As far as I'm aware, there were no Croatian forces that area. If the term "Ustasha" is being used to refer to Muslim forces, then it would seem to indicate that this document is giving an order to crush those forces in that area. To me, it's a little bit of a curiosity as to why that language should be used, but it also little makes difference to me in the sense that there was no doubt that Serbian forces were attempting to overwhelm and eradicate non-Serbian forces of whatever kind, but we assume usually Bosnian government military forces in that area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Non-Serb forces, therefore.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We could say that. Dr. Gow, I would like to show you another document now, D33, Defence Exhibit D33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you tendering this previous document in evidence, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered and admitted in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D75.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, this is another directive of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. This is a directive of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, dated the 3rd of August, 1992. It's a logistics directive for providing logistics support, operations number 3. Can you look at page 5, item 7? It reads "Quartermaster Security."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The translation says "Quartermaster Support." If may also say that I hope there's a better original copy than this one for the files and the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree. It's something that, unfortunately, we have to learn and live with. Some of them are in an awful state.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Dr. Gow, this is a document that we received, and a very poor copy from the OTP. I can only quote the section of the document which says: "In carrying out the quartermaster support for the units, the main way of obtaining supplies is to rely on the capacities of the logistics supports and use the supplies of civilian bakers, slaughterhouses, farms, cooperatives, commodity reserves belonging to companies, farms and agricultural communities, as well as individual producers." Dr. Gow, does this document not show that the territory controlled by the army of Republika Srpska, to a large extent, was militarised and used, in fact, for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not clear about the question. Forgive me, I think I was busy trying to read and I missed something. Would you mind repeating it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will quote again: "In carrying out the support for quartermasters in units used the following capacities: All supplies from the territory --" I'm only reading out the relevant bit, "civilian bakers, slaughterhouses, warehouses belonging to companies, the commodity reserves belonging to companies through agricultural farms, cooperatives, individual companies." The question related to that was: Does this document not indicate that the area controlled by the army of Republika Srpska was, to a high degree, militarised in the sense that even the commodity reserves belonging to farms, individual manufacturers and companies, were being used for military purposes? Is that something that your research, too, has shown?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am confused -- sorry, because there's a difference -- there are additional parts in the English translation that I don't seem to see in what I can see of the original, and so I've been confused between those two things. The original would seem to go with what you have said in terms of it was expected that you would look to get military -- to meet military needs in terms of food and so forth by turning to the local community. Unless I'm in the wrong place, there seems to be a reference to federal and republican in the translation. Am I in the wrong place? Which I can't see in the original. And I think that's my confusion, because I think in the first place I was reading this and thinking it was a reference to the relationship with Belgrade. Am I in the right place?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Dr. Gow, can you please look at the section under 7A, 7A.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under 7A.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I've found the place. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It confirms that they would use local suppliers for military needs, but I don't think there would be anything enormously surprising in that, and that's why I thought you'd said, see, in the first place, and I was looking at the other part. I was expecting that the issue was just in getting supplies from across the border rather than this. But certainly it indicates that they would be looking to local providers to meet the needs of the military, but it really doesn't seem surprising --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a normality, it's a proposition of requisition, and basically, it's more or else.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry for the confusion, or my part in it, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you, Dr. Gow. You do know that the Drina Corps, in November 1992, was, in fact, within the compensation of the army of Republika Srpska, covering the municipalities of Bratunac, Srebrenica, Zvornik, and Vlasenica. I will now proceed to show you a document of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, dated the 19th of November, 1992, signed by General Ratko Mladic. The relevant pages are 3, 6, and 7. In the English, the last sentence on page 2, Dr. Gow, page 3 of the B/C/S original, and the English begins at the bottom of page 2: "Meanwhile, the Drina Corps was formed. Its command and units have been brought up to the highest level of combat readiness and successfully crushing the enemy in Podrinje. The air force and anti-aircraft defence have achieved maximum results in supporting the ground forces, which, according to the number of sorties, has not been recorded anywhere in the world." Therefore, Dr. Gow, this is about Podrinje, which is of relevance to our case. Dr. Gow, has your research shown that the air force was permanently active throughout this area at that period of time, and does this document not seem to confirm that precisely?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly the case that there was constant air activity. The document indicates that there was some kind of air support in the area. I'm not sure what else you might want me to say beyond that. But if you tell me anything else you might want, I'd be happy to try and help.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to ask you this: Your research, has it not shown -- or rather, has it shown that the Muslim forces, too, had in fact an air force, or was this air force under consideration here a Serb-controlled air force, receiving support from forces coming from Yugoslavia that were then carrying out bombardments?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did have a very limited air capability, primarily helicopters. Most of the air activity most of the time through the war was -- did involve helicopters rather than fixed-wing aircraft. That was because the UN Security Council put in place at one stage, a little bit later, what was called a no-fly zone. But it was difficult to enforce the no-fly zone against helicopters. I can say that as far as my recollection and research goes, there was actually fixed-wing air activity at this time, and in this area. But I'm not sure if we can go far beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, speaking of the Podrinje area, has your research shown that the area was bombed from Belgrade between 1992 and April 1993 which is when the demilitarisation campaign took place?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that it was bombed by Belgrade, although I think it's likely that the aircraft were a Belgrade-controlled aircraft, i.e. relating to the VJ but I can't confirm that because I simply don't know. I can confirm that in -- I mean, this document is dated November 1992. I'm prepared to accept that there will have been air action at that stage. Certainly in those -- after the turn of the year, in the first part of 1993, there was certainly UN monitors reporting air action in this area with fixed-wing aircraft, without necessarily designating whether they were VJ or aircraft from the VRS. But simply that there was fixed-wing aircraft activity by Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Gow. I would now like to draw your attention to page 6 of the Bosnian version, which is page 5 in English, item -- or subsection D. Subsection D talks about the objectives of the Drina Corps. It reads: "The Drina Corps, from its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad, the dam, Zvornik, and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on them, and force them to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population. First offer the able-bodied and armed men to surrender, and if they refuse, destroy them." Dr. Gow, do you agree that as early as November 1992, there was a clear-cut plan to eliminate the enclaves of Srebrenica, Cerska and Konjevic Polje, or rather, to crush the entire population of the area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly agree that as early as November 1992 there was that intention. I don't know about crushing the Muslim population but certainly to remove it from the territory. And I would go further and say it was from a considerably earlier stage than November 1992. I might take this opportunity. Yesterday the question was raised about paramilitary forces, Arkan's Serbian volunteer guard, the Tigers, going, entering the town of Srebrenica, and the date. I took the liberty last night of checking what the date was because I said I wasn't sure. It was the 18th of April. I think if you can go back to the 18th of April, 1992, you can see that there was the intention to do that as well. That this document confirms that that intention was also there in November, I've got no problem accepting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want this clear, Madam Vidovic and Dr. Gow, because Madam Vidovic used the verb "crush" and you have diverted that -- from that and restricted yourself, it's seen at least in my opinion, to "remove." The two are not the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which is why I made the distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. The two are not the same. So, I would like you to be very specific in answering this question, and I would put the question: What do you understand, first of all, by "crush the Muslim population"? How do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my concern with the word "crush" is that it could have many meanings, one of which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I'm putting the question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Crush them militarily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be to crush militarily. But this is a specific reference to civilian population. It could be to roll them over. It could be to remove any sense of spirit and morale. It could be to eliminate. It could simply be to overwhelm and take over. I was making the distinction simply because the translation says, "force them out," and the original says something equivalent to that, which is "napustiti prostore", to be clean, to be moved out of the area. So it was -- that's why I make this distinction. If that satisfies Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- stick to whatever point in time you would like to fix. What do you agree was the intention of the Serbian authorities vis-a-vis the Muslim civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The intention was to create a territory on which there would be no Muslim population. That is absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be sufficient. Dr. Gow, I will now ask you to look at page 7 of the same document, item 6, the support for combat activities. And there's another issue I'll ask you about it. "A. Intelligence and security support."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the page again? I missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Page 7.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the original?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In both, both versions. The subheading under A, "intelligence and security support." The second line in the paragraph reads as follows, and I'll quote: "Since the Muslim and HVO forces cannot put up a more organised resistance to larger units, they are forced to resort to guerilla warfare." It goes on to say, there's a continuation to that, but I would like to ask you the following, Mr. Gow: Has your study shown that the Muslims in the area waged such a warfare, therefore, guerilla warfare?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it has, and that it -- that in the period we've been discussing, this period, late 1992 and early 1993, in military terms it was quite successful. It seemed that in the region as a whole, a degree of control, albeit against significantly weak Serbian forces at that time, but still a significant area was widened under the control of the so-called guerilla forces fighting against the Serbian forces. And of course, I don't think it's a secret that your client, the defendant's name, is widely associated with that campaign.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were they forced to wage such a warfare due to the significant lack in armaments and resources as compared to the other side?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had, if they were going to fight from a weaker position against a stronger opponent, to adopt an asymmetric strategy. I made reference, again, to this I think, on the first day of evidence. We were asked about the old Yugoslav defence system. That was predicated on the idea of falling back in-depth and using a Territorial Defence guerilla strategy as a way of combatting a significantly stronger aggressor. And what was unusual in the context of the war in Yugoslavia was that this was just about the only case in which that strategy, which makes more sense from a weaker position, was actually used. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the Bosnian theatre, for the rest of the war, seemed to try to fight on equal terms and not to do it very well in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I move to my next question, could this document please be assigned a number as an exhibit and be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered and received in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D76. If I make a mistake in the sequence, registrar, please draw my attention immediately. Yes, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may just add a little bit to that last answer, and connect it with one of the documents we were shown yesterday, the extract from the book on alleged atrocities against ethnic Serbs. That book was produced in relation to the success of the Muslim forces in Eastern Bosnia, and it was widely reported at that time that there had been sometimes described as massacres and killings, and certainly what were described as reprisals. So I think that's the context to understand in the connection between those two pieces of evidence, in case that it's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, can I ask you a question in relation to that. Have you ever, in your studies, come across a piece of information that Muslims were impaling people? Did you come across any information that can be substantiated or corroborated to that effect, regardless of whether it's in Visegrad or somewhere else? I'm referring to the article that you saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back to the headline about impaling, I'm not aware of any specific example of impaling. But I'm not sure I would necessarily be aware of an example, even if it had taken place. So I don't think that excludes the possibility that there were actions being taken -- I'm not saying whether or not, it's not my place to say whether or not such actions were taking place, but simply that there were reports of activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But you have not come across such an example have you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the act of impaling, I haven't, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- necessarily --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's clear. Thank you, Dr. Gow. I'll move onto my next question. In your book, the Triumph of the Lack of Will, pages 141 and 142, if you could please be shown these. In these pages you focused on the mass-scale Serb campaign against the small, predominantly Muslim town of Srebrenica in Eastern Bosnia. You explain that the Serb campaign was aimed at getting rid of the Muslims in the valley where there were some 40.000 refugees that had fled from other regions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a paragraph on the page which deals with the circumstances in Srebrenica which gave rise to the UN safe area there, or to the originally agreed Red Cross safe area which then became one of the UN Security Council designated safe areas. I think it's important to understand that it's in the context of what gave rise to safe areas rather than simply about Srebrenica. But that's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I merely wanted to ask you whether you came across the figure that there were as many refugees in the valley?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of refugees, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think yesterday --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think somewhere yesterday there was a document that said 80.000. I said that I rather thought it was a smaller figure than that. But there were tens of thousands of refugees, I mean, and that's the key point.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that sometimes figures referred to the town of Srebrenica only and sometimes they include the enclaves of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and the surrounding villages and hamlets. Do you agree that sometimes different data presented to this reason, because you were referring to the town of Srebrenica itself, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the town of Srebrenica, but I think most of the data that is found and recorded in the UN system also relates to the town of Srebrenica. There was a period when there was a wider area of control, but for most of the time there was a much narrower area of control because of the Serbian disposition, which means that Srebrenica was the focus. And that's where, for the most part, refugees were. We should also point out, I think, that most of the people in Srebrenica by this time were displaced people, were refugees, and that many of the original inhabitants of Srebrenica had left after the original attacks in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. Furthermore, in your book, you wrote that the destruction campaign started with the intention of eliminating the Muslim communities in Eastern Bosnia. I will quote a small part of it: "Not only was the VRS commander, General Mladic, exerting pressure on Eastern Bosnia through heavy artillery, he was also denying passage to convoys of humanitarian aid of UN, and for these reasons UNPROFOR and the broader international community it represented was faced with demands for action to prevent massacre and starvation in the region." Dr. Gow, my question is as follows: Does this mean that there was an actual risk of starvation and violent death for the people in Srebrenica at this period in time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it does, and that was the intention of the Serbian campaign, as I think we've been making clear throughout the whole of this system. It was to remove one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. I will present you with a document of the War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica of 24th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, could, please, these two pages from Dr. Gow's book be assigned a number and be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, being an extract from the witness's book, "Triumph of the Lack of Will: International Diplomacy and the Yugoslav War" is being tendered and admitted in evidence, and is being marked as Defence Exhibit D77.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You Honour, may I?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Gow would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for indulging me once more. Seeing as you're taking these two pages as evidence, I just point out the reference to the third line down on page 142, which is to the reports about the reprisal actions that I mentioned earlier and the reports of summary executions, just to note that that's within the evidence being presented here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the footnote that goes with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had already noted that paragraph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me for presuming.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, can you please look at the documents of the War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica of the 24th of January 1993, number 179/3. The document is entitled "Appeal," and the second paragraph reads: "We are all hungry. More than half of us are sick, and only in the course of yesterday, 14 residents died." The following paragraph starts with the line: "The Srebrenica area is an area where hungry and sick people live, an area of death, and nobody is concerned about saving this particular area of Bosnia-Herzegovina and helping the suffering population." The sixth paragraph goes on to say: "Another danger like the sword of Damocles is over Srebrenica, and that's the VRS stationed at Bajna Basta and the occupied Skelani, both upper and down the Drina river, that is to say, the Uzice Corps." Does this document reflect the actual reality that Srebrenica was faced with, as described by you in your book?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just ask to check which document we're dealing with? I can't find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the things you've said, I'd concur, but they don't seem to relate to the document that is in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I've been trying to follow what you've been reading, but I can't find it in the document that I have.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we check the ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is possible that there was a mistake. I was referring to the document by the War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica, number 179/3, of January 24, 1993, entitled "Appeal."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So ERN 571918, whereas the document we had was a different ERN.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, 918.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the one I have here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we have, however, is 922, not 918. July -- at the top it says July 15th, 2003, but then the document itself is dated 25th of January of 1993. The War Presidency, the reference number is 180/93. Let me see. No, it's definitely not the same. No, it's not the same. What we have been given is not the same. We have been given the following, the subsequent document, the War Presidency document 180/93, while we should have document 179/93. So we will return these.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, excuse me, Madam Vidovic. Could we have a correct copy of the document he's referring to now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have one either, Ms. Sellers. We could make photocopies of the document if proper photocopies are not already available. In the meantime, Ms. Sellers, you can follow from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest, Ms. Vidovic, that you start all over again, that you repeat your question, basically, because now, sort of, we've lost track.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the document should be raised on the ELMO so that -- yes, okay, that's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, this is an appeal by the War Presidency of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph bolded here reads as follows: "All of us are hungry. More than half of us are sick. Only yesterday 14 inhabitants died." Then the second bolded passage: "The area of Srebrenica is an area of hunger and sickness, of death. Nobody is concerned about saving this part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and help the suffering population." Could you please lift the document on the ELMO. "Another danger, like the sword of Damocles, hovers above Srebrenica. It is the army of the so-called Federal Republic of Yugoslavia located in Bajna Basta and in the occupied area of Skelani, as well as upstream and downstream of the Drina river, that is to say, the Uzice Corps." Dr. Gow, does this not reflect the actual situation as it was in Srebrenica, and does it also reflect what you yourself wrote in your book?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It, indeed, reflects both those things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please make sure you limit your answer to this specific period of time that we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It refers to the period of time we're dealing with, January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this document of the War Presidency that we've discussed be assigned a number and be admitted into evidence as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We still don't have a copy of it. But when we have it, that document will be marked as Defence Exhibit D78. D78. Yes, I take it, Dr. Gow, that you would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yet again, I'm sorry, and just for clarity if we've finished with this document otherwise, si to note and confirm that Bajna Basta is in Serbia, that the name Skelani refers to a location in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so we're talking about forces from Serbia operating in a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, across the other side of the Drina, and firing as well from the other side of the Drina into it. And then when it says Uzice Corps, the Uzice Corps is an army of what was designated the VJ, the army of Yugoslavia, and indeed the General Ojdanic, who was later to be the commander in Kosovo and then federal defence, actually, at the time of the operations in Kosovo. Just to provide context for all those things. I'm very sorry. Sorry. General Ojdanic whose name is on the screen here, O-j-d-a-n-i-c - okay - who is referred to here as commander of the Uzice Corps, was later to be commander of the 3rd army over Kosovo, and after that Belgrade defence secretary at the time of the Kosovo operations in 1998/1999 -- or 1999, sorry. That's just to give context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic -- yes, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I've been assured that we'll get copies of this exhibit. It's just that we did -- it appears that the Defence, when they did show us some of their Defence exhibits prior, we do have a copy in B/C/S. I'll just note that our copy seems ends with a comma, so I don't know whether there should be two pages to it. We would very much like to know if there's a second page, and as the Defence -- we don't object to its admission at all into evidence. We would like to know who signed or somehow verified the original, and then the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is the document? Could you please bring it over? Thank you. So, Ms. Sellers, the original in the Serbian language, Serbian-Croat language, has an ERN number -- it consists of two pages, and ERN number 01857918 to 19. It does have a signature on the second page, but the signature is -- it seems to be affixed to the part of the document which says "received via an amateur radio station in Sarajevo, received by Ilijas Omerovic." But as you see, the B/C/S original consists of two pages, okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The English translation, instead, consists of one page, consists of one page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will need photocopies of these. Thank you. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 28 in your statement of 9th September 2004 that you gave to the OTP, and that was admitted into evidence yesterday, you speak of increased actions in Podrinje in the beginning of 1993. You mentioned thousands of soldiers of Yugoslavia and paramilitary forces crossing the Drina river with more than 100 tanks and APCs. Was this a part of the campaign to destroy the Muslim population in Podrinje?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a part of the Serbian campaign that we've been discussing throughout, to remove the Serbian population -- sorry, to remove the Muslim population and to secure control of those territories by doing so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the document by UNHCR that we will show you. UNHCR update on the former Yugoslavia, dated 12 February 1993. Could you please look at the second paragraph, which reads: "In a letter to the leader of the Bosnian Serbs, Radovan Karadzic and Ms. Ogata," that is to say, the high commissioner for refugees, "said UNHCR had been pressing for weeks for clearance to deliver aid to the enclaves where more than 100.000 people are suffering untold hardship due to the military blockade." These reports that refer to the Muslim enclaves, did they cause concern on the part of the international community, and the intention of the international community?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. Quite clearly they did. This document is one example of it. The mention of the UN-declared safe areas and the Red Cross agreement prior to that safe area, we've already mentioned, are all part of the attention that is being drawn to Eastern Bosnia because of the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gow, this report is dated 12 February 1993, therefore a bit before the safe zone was actually established.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, it's before that. But I think there was concern and attention even before that. I think you'll find -- you can look at a trail of attention going back to late 1992, and certainly from the beginning of 1993, all part of that attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you, Dr. Gow. I have perhaps two or three more questions for you. This concern was, therefore, so extensive that the representatives of the international community who were on the ground cautioned about the possibility that the Serbs would carry out genocide in the area as early as at that time. I will now show you a document and draw your attention to one section to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Dr. Gow please be shown this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, could this previous document be assigned a number and admitted as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the document, being UNHCR update on ex-Yugoslavia, dated 12th February 1993, is being tendered and received in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D79.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you'll permit me yet again just to add -- draw to your attention, not presuming that you won't read the whole of the documents anyway. Further down there's also the reference to the UNHCR being denied access to Sastakanica [phoen], with the one exception of opening up a one-way channel. This is all part of the same context of the campaign that the document has evidence relating to it should be noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we have another document now. Do we have it on the ELMO, or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you please look at the following section, paragraph 11. Paragraph 11: "If free passage with transport cannot be arranged for the refugees in the Srebrenica pocket within the next 7 to 14 days, indications are that the Serbs will carry out a genocidal cleansing of the enclave, resulting in the potential death of up to 80.000 human beings." Dr. Gow, is it true that the campaign of genocidal cleansing of the enclave mentioned in paragraph 11, which was in March 1993, was of great concern to the international community?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was of great concern, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this concern was a real one, wasn't it, based on realistic circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what an unreal concern would be. But absolutely, it was a real concern. They were facing the prospect of what -- of how to deal with tens of thousands of human beings, whether they would try to look after them in situ or try to move them in some other way to safety, and what the implications that there would be for moving them to safety, implicitly assisting with the process of ethnic cleansing, or saving lives, which is one of the dilemmas faced by the international effort throughout. But I think the judgement made in the final paragraph, in the final sentence of that paragraph, they are unlikely to stop this offensive until the enclave is cleared one way or another. I think it is probably borne out by the events in 1995, that the intention was always there and it was only a matter of time until the point where it could be executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we may two further questions for Dr. Gow. It won't take long. I believe this is a good time for a break, however. And can this document just please be assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being tendered and admitted in evidence and being marked as Defence Exhibit D80. Just one question before we rise for the break. I would like confirmation as to the date of this document. I know that if you look at the top right, there is a date, time, 20, 2355A, and then what appears to be March 1993. I want a confirmation of that. Are we talking of March 1993, or are we talking of some other year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you wish, Your Honour, I can confirm that this is March 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean, I thought so, but I wanted a confirmation from one of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if I may add yet again, this irritating witness who's wanting to say more than they probably should, but in paragraph 8 of the previous page, which I've put up on the ELMO, in reference to some of the things I've been saying at other times, the UNPROFOR, that's the UN peace force, report here indicates assistance from Serbia with artillery fire and ground attack, aircraft as well. Just add further little bit of evidence to the things that I've been saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Basically we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to thank Dr. Gow, and we have no further questions. We conferred during the break and we decided to ask no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there re-examination, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to say that there would be no re-examination. We would like to place on the record that we do feel that the second half of the cross-examination has, in essence, not been a cross-examination under Rule 90, particularly (H)(ii). At this point in time, due to the nature of the entire cross-examination, we would like to renew the request, and we can do that in writing and correspondence, to ask the Defence would stipulate at least to the fact of an armed conflict on the territory, as amended in the new indictment. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is without the internationality character.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the indictment no longer sets forth the internationality but I believe that the Defence has stated earlier said they were not interested in the internationality aspects. So, therefore, we would renew our request just to armed conflict as stated in the general allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's up to Defence -- to the Defence to decide upon. So I take it there are no questions from the Prosecution to the witness. Judge Brydensholt would like to put some questions to you, Dr. Gow, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: You mentioned the very first day that there was no command structure in 1992, there was no command structure on the Muslim side, as far as I remember. It was more of a top organisation, and you even said that up -- oh, yes, sorry. You even said that up until 1995, it was not still really in order, the command structure. Would you elaborate a bit on that? What do you know, if at all, about the Muslim side, and on what basis do you say that they had no real command structure? It was more ad hoc.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think -- well, let me be clear when I say -- when I was talking about the degree of formation within the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the levels of competence and organisation, I would not wish to suggest that there was no command structure from the outset. At least from the declaration to form the army on the 15th of April, there was a command structure. And within the old Territorial Defence system under the control of the Bosnian authority, or areas under the Muslim control, there was certainly command and control. What I was suggesting in that, in the reference to 1995 was about the character of the army of Bosnia and Hercegovina and its formation. By the end of 1995, in my judgement, and in those -- the judgement perhaps of those with perhaps even greater expertise, predominantly British military professionals who had experience in Bosnia with whom I've discussed these issues, the Bosnian army did not have a strategic-level capability. The joint operations between the Croatian army and the Bosnian army, which took place in the final phases of the war, in 1995, indeed later 1994, the first of them, were ones where the strategic level -- and if you recall at one point I was discussing the different levels. You have policy, grand strategic, strategic, operational, and then tactical levels. That at that level of relating politics to the use of armed force, I think it can be said that even by the end of the armed hostilities in Bosnia, that forming Bosnian army still didn't have the full rounded coherence and competence to operate at a strategic level. That doesn't mean that it didn't have command and control and that it didn't have structures. I was talking about the character of the army and its capacities to act as an army. By the end, it certainly could -- it certainly had an operational capability. At the times where it's apparently sought to act strategically, it usually failed. And even when there was small initial successes, the VRS, under General Mladic, would then be able, after a short time, quite easily to be able to push it back. So when I say about -- I want to get clear that what I -- whatever it was exactly that I said, that I'm talking about command and control in a full sense of a fully functioning and operating armed force. And I think that by 1995 and the end of armed hostilities, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina still was not an army which fully had that character. It certainly had effective command and control arrangements, if you're talking about the structures within the armed forces, the organisation, and a degree of communication and ordering. And I should say that it even had that going back to 1992. But it was an evolving process. So when the army was initially formed, for example, it was designated as having forces in places like Mostar, and having a corps command relating to Mostar, but there was no force in Mostar de facto. So on one part you had people appointed to positions, but there was no actual role that they were playing in the place and the way they were supposed to be playing it. In the course of 1992, as this Bosnian army was forming on the basis of the Patriotic League and the Territorial Defence forces, things were being changed, coherence was coming together. That's why you've got one declaration in April, you've got further steps in May, you have the formation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Could you tell me what further steps in May? I'm aware --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Well, I think it was in May there was a further law/declaration on the structure of the armed forces which gave rise to putting in place administrative districts. These were later supplanted by the military districts and corps in the August documents that we saw in evidence. In July, there was the formation of tactical groups. These were groups used by the old JNA for two purposes, either for a specific objective of bringing together different elements of forces otherwise not subordinated to the same command, or for some speculative operations where no formal regular force was in a position to be able to carry it out. And in some sense, as the tactical groups used by the Bosnian army in this period -- it was a part of this evolving character, the ones which were responding to the lack of a fully formed authority while the work, clear command and control arrangements were coming down from the presidency through General Halilovic, as part of this organisation. There were clear areas where there were elements of uncertainty, where people were appointed in roles such as coordinator, not in normally formally recognised military position. But the point there was that they were in an evolving and adapting situation. They were the ones who were able to use either qualifications or personality, experience, whatever it might be, to take part in forming this army. I think we should always be clear that there were structures, that there were command and control structures, but they were not necessarily functioning as a whole and complete armed force throughout -- in this period, certainly through to about November 1992. But that does not mean to say that there was not command and control. I think it also should be understood that forces operating outside those formal structures where the formal structures had not yet been able to take effect, and Eastern Bosnia for some of the time can be one of those, were still operating under a system of command and control that related to the notions of guerilla warfare, to Territorial Defence, and the political-military relations that went with that. And when we come to late 1992, we've talked a bit about the operations of the Muslim guerilla force in Eastern Bosnia. In part that can be seen as simply -- almost self-organising local initiative, but it clearly relates to the 2nd Corps in Tuzla --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interpreters and transcribers alike. When we come to the end of 1992, in the autumn, when these operations are being successful in creating area under Muslim control in Eastern Bosnia, and I think at one point also Srebrenica and Zepa even become joint for a time, the context of that is fairly weak Serbian forces, because the Serbian forces are concentrating on the Posavina corridor, to which we've made reference as the lifeline for the Serbian project across the north. In that context, I think we have to understand that there was coordination at the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993 between the forces operating in Srebrenica and Cerska, and those of 2 Corps command. And there was an overall strategic position where the intention, by using the guerilla forces and their operations, aside from the guerilla strategy and controlling the territory itself, was diversionary, that is, to put demands on Serbian forces while 2 Corps watched an operation north to try and cut the Posavina Corridor, which, indeed, it did for a period around Christmastime 1992 for about 15 days, and then again in January for a few days later. So all this is part of an overall structure. So I don't know if I've made this any clearer at all, but I think what I want to make clear is there were formal structures, there were formal plans. But at the same time, when I made that comment about the character of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was that the structures themselves were evolving and changing and were forming to become something reasonably fixed, which I think you can say happened in the second half of 1992. But the full character of the army still, in my judgement, and, as I say, that of others with greater expertise in professional terms, was that it still didn't have the qualities of a full army by the end of the war. It doesn't mean that there wasn't command and control, or that there were no structures for command and control. All that -- wherever you even had guerilla operations, they were not part of an overall strategic approach relating to the very formal structures, such as that example of 2 Corps and the attempt to cut the Posavina Corridor by using the guerilla operations coordinated to put pressure on Serbian forces to weaken Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you. We have seen that on the Serb side, they maintained that under the Serb authority should not only be those parts of Bosnia where they actually were in the majority, but also those parts where they would have been if it not had been due to the acts under the Second World War. How does that affect the eastern part of Bosnia, which we are dealing with in this case? Were they actually landscapes, geographical areas, where the Serbs, up until and during the Second World War, had been in clear majority? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know enough to pass serious comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly say that the weight of the -- of that question goes to northwestern Bosnia and the area with Croatia on the other side of it, Kardun. Whether any of it goes to Eastern Bosnia, I would hesitate to say in a situation like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: We have heard your explanation about this Serb project, and we have heard about the changes which took place in their constitution regarding the people of Serbia. Have you found any written documentation regarding this cleansing policy? You have described how it took place, how they thought to get rid, somehow, of the non-Serb population. Have you seen any written orders or declarations or proposals saying what exactly should be done with the Muslims, for instance.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand Your Honour correctly, we had one of those earlier this morning which spoke specifically about removing the civilian Muslim population from the territories we were talking about in this case. We have -- there were other cases where you see the term "cleansing," "etnicko ciscejne", being introduced. And I think the understanding of that has to be that the intention, wherever it is to be used, is to clear those territories of the non-ethnic Serbs, and certainly of any non-ethnic Serbs who are not prepared to live under an ethnic Serb policy. The term was originally coined and, as I recall, reported in the Financial Times in -- I'd have to go and look for it -- by Vojislav Seselj, as far as I'm aware, in 1992 as a way of describing what it was that was taking place. Vojislav Seselj was a Serbian politician who was also leader of one of the prominent paramilitary formations that we discussed also, the Beli Orlovi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Do you remember we discussed the meaning of the word "crush," to be crushed.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And my question is: Have you seen in any detail a description of what should be done? You mentioned that it could have many meanings, but has anybody said what actually should be done to the non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with reference to the word "crushed," if I may, that was because the translation that came through said "crushed," which was not the original word, with respect to the translators. I just wanted to be clear that that -- that the word shouldn't be taken through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word -- a word close to "crushed," "unistenje." Is one that was used by Radovan Karadzic in the parliament in October 1992 -- sorry, 1991, in the discussions regarding Bosnian sovereignty and the declaration of sovereignty, which is taken by many as a warning that the Serbs -- that the Muslims will be destroyed, if this goes through. I say it's taken by many. Again, in retro -- ex post facto, it certainly can be read as indicating what the intention was. I always have to caution that political rhetoric in the heat of the moment in parliament might not necessarily be setting an agenda. But I don't think we can have any doubt, leaving aside where the references come, and you can -- you could piece together these references, that what makes it clear is the consistent and coordinated action on the ground. It's action which cannot take place without preparation and planning. Anybody who knows the first thing about trying to organise, probably, a party let alone the use of armed forces and campaigns of this kind including the creation of detention centres, the laying out of the paperwork to go with it, the use of integrated networks to transfer people from one place to another, including from places in the so-called Republika Srpska, into Serbia proper, Serbia as in Serbia Montenegro, this is all part of something which is just so completely consistent and coordinated that it could not happen without it being clearly planned and understood, but quite possibly through verbal communication a lot of the time, because many things were done through an oral manner, because you generally don't want to leave a written record of giving specific instructions for some of the things we discuss. Although over the years, as I say, little pieces, even in writing, have emerged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I also have some questions.
