I would have had the same question as Judge Brydensholt, but I have some additional ones, and they follow the sequence of the examination and the cross-examination, starting with a question with regard to the ethnicity, the ethnic composition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps it would be helpful to get the Prosecution document 367, if it could be placed on the -- what do you call it, ELMO? I still don't know what it means, ELMO. Perhaps I can already start with my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Electric monitor, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: You told us that the Muslims make up about 40 per cent of the population --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said 44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. In this area. But if you see Prosecution Exhibit 367, you remember when you told us that the area where Muslims live should not be -- should be -- wait?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Apparently there is a problem with this document. Are you sure it's 367? Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It was a map. Do you remember the map you had? I think it was described as areas which are mainly occupied by Muslims or mainly by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the military control one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes. And you told us that the Muslim region should not be considered as a comprehensive one, but there have been corridors in between, or areas where it was not possible to go from one to the other. But if you have this map in view, you get the impression that Serbs are occupying much more of the territory than the Muslims, so I think that the Serbian occupation is more than 60 per cent compared to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't want to interrupt Your Honour. But we do have it. We'll put it up on Sanction just for the benefit of the view, certainly until the registrar has the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It might be this one now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, 367. We had it in colour. There is a colour version of it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now what was -- the Republika Srpska, if I'm correct in assuming, was thought to be part of Eastern Bosnia, not Western Bosnia, although the western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was occupied by Serbs. Now, was the idea of the project, of the new project, that Republika Srpska should also encompass the western part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. If that wasn't clear from what I said, I'm quite surprises, but forgive me for not being clear. The Republika Srpska was the whole of the territory to which the Bosnian Serbs aspired, included all of the territory that can be seen on this map as under Serbian control. And bear in mind, this is not -- this is not an ethnic distribution map, this is a map indicating areas of military control, although there is a bit of consistency between those two factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Why is the --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this shows an area, all of which is taken to become -- to compose the Republika Srpska, but there are aspirations to territory which is not under Serbian control, as shown on this map, or what will be Republika Srpska. But certainly western -- the western parts, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Could you still leave it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we have the coloured one, it's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: For my purpose, I think it's enough to have this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have the coloured one now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, if you -- now, what was the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have the coloured one? I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to go on video mode.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But this -- the red parts, which are the Serbian parts, I think, would be much more -- or the green parts, the Muslim parts, would be much less than 40 per cent. Would it mean that the Muslims would have been driven out of these areas as well, so they would have less than 40 per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand the question correctly, and forgive me if I'm going in the wrong direction here, I have to point out, just to be absolutely clear, this is a map showing military control, not showing ethnic proportionality and density in the population. Therefore, to read a sense of proportionality on ethnicity from this map wouldn't necessarily be the right thing to do. What the map shows is the areas under Serbian control, and indeed under the control of others. Those areas under Serbian control had almost the entire Muslim population removed from them; in some cases completely, in some cases as of that time not completely. The area under Serbian control represents probably about two-thirds to 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The area under Muslim or Bosnian government control represents significantly less than 40, 44 per cent of the territory. But to be clear, that's areas under control rather than a reflection of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But what was the goal of the new project? Was the goal that all parts which have been militarily controlled by Serbs should be -- later on be part of a Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And if I could ask to get the map back again? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is. Press the next button, video evidence, please, and you should get it there.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. If -- am I able -- my indication does nothing here. But if you can -- thank you. It's probably easier. It was certainly the case that the territory under control at this time should be part of the Republika Srpska. The intention was also quite clearly that this territory in the east under Muslim control should be part of it, and the aspiration was also, first, to cut a line along the river Krivaj, which runs approximately there, and then to mop up this Muslim-controlled area here. So, in fact, the territory of the Republika Srpska, if the whole project had been successful, would also have included this much broader swathe around Tuzla as well. So the territory that was intended to be part of it was not necessarily the territory that was under control, and the territory which has become part of Republika Srpska, the entity within Bosnia-Herzegovina under the general framework for peace agreement, is less than the territory under control here as well, because, as a result of operations, joint operations by Croatian forces, and Bosnian forces, first of all, and then negotiations, Dayton, the territory was reduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question has to do with the hostilities you talked about, and you mentioned that the M-U-P, or MUP, played a significant role in the very origins of the conflicts in central Bosnia. What do you mean? This is literally taken from the transcript. "Played a significant role in the very origins of the conflicts in central Bosnia." What do you mean by "significant role"? What type of role was it? That the police --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it possible to get a wider context of the quotation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It was in connection with the start of conflicts between the Muslim and Serb population, and that the Serb -- the Muslims have been provoked, yes? In this context, you mentioned that the MUP played a significant role in the origins of this conflict. What kind of role was it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP was integrated as part of the crisis headquarters, or the leaders of the MUP were integrated as part of the crisis headquarters that were formed by the SDS party organisation, and their role was to provide information, which some other people would describe as intelligence, on the local non-Serbs, to draw lists of those non-Serbs who would be potential leaders or otherwise potential -- significant in opposing the takeover, to ensure that they would be the first ones to be detained, or in some cases, they were killed, to be removed from the scene. They would then be part of the process in identifying others and preparing the bureaucratic elements of takeover and elimination through removal, one way or another, of the non-Serbs in the community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question has to do with the awareness of the population of what was going on. You have been very cautious in saying that you have only dealt with the strategical level, so to say, but not so much with the implementation in practice. But nevertheless, what, to your knowledge, what was the populace, the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina be able to learn and hear about what was going on in other parts of the country? For instance, could the Serb villagers know what was going on in Muslim villages, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly. When I was expressing caution in terms of expertise that my work is principally of a strategic character, lies at the strategic level, I think I also said that I don't know nothing about the tactical level. Sometimes you can't understand the strategic without knowing something of the tactical. But it's that I didn't have extensive, necessarily, expertise. Sometimes I would, sometimes I wouldn't. But at the level of what the population could or would know, there's no doubt that it was possible to know, and no doubt that people knew of things that were happening. Now, whether they believed the reports that they would hear in some cases or not, I think, has to be open to question. Had I not been in the -- those Croatian-Bosnian border areas at the time that this started, and I was, I would say that I probably would have treated reports of what people were saying as they were coming up with scepticism as well. But it's when you get such a density in the same kind of reporting when there's no possibility for it have just been word of mouth and repeating -- at later stages there's people who know things because they've heard something, not because this happened to them firsthand. And the reporting that the European Community Monitoring Mission and the UN forces in Croatia, who were observing from across the border at that time, I think that's -- that people had ways of knowing because not only were there newspapers, of course, and television reporting some of this, but a lot would spread through word of mouth. And one part of the idea inherent in ethnic cleansing is that inducing fear and inducing people to move because of what they've heard of what is happening, is a key component.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge and estimation, do you think that it's possible that something happens in a village, let's say 10 to 15 kilometres away, that the neighbouring villagers do not know what is going on in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably going to the very limits. I should have thought that most of the time it would be hard, over a fairly short period of time, for word not to pass. But I would hesitate to say with absolute conviction that that had to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My next question is more or less on this problem of the perception of the population. We have heard about the mobilisation order of April 16th, 1992. Now, these orders, which have been taken by the municipality or by some army people, is it possible that the people also knew of this, or was only the order taken by a certain majority but that the population at large did not be acquainted with it -- did not become acquainted with it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that would depend on the means of communication, how the order was made -- was made open to public knowledge. Without knowing the detail, we can't be absolutely sure. I would expect that something like that anyway would be reported on television and radio and in newspapers in some way. Certainly those in positions of authority in that situation, going back to the old -- the whole defence system and fabric, where it was assumed that 85 per cent of the people would have some kind of a role, whether civilian or military, in that defence operation, that there would be people with responsibilities and authority who certainly would know and, one way or another, would communicate as much as they thought others would need to know, even if others weren't reading about the general mobilisation. And I think I said on the first day of evidence that probably everybody would know where they were supposed to go when there was a mobilisation and what they were supposed to do in their little bit. It wouldn't necessarily mean that they would have a more global understanding of the whole of what was happening. But they know, I go and report here and I do my little bit. Whether I'm going to be kind of a civilian defence, protecting the local town hall, or whether I'm going to be going into some MUP unit to provide some more significant role, using either information or armed force, or to an element of the Territorial Defence. They would know where they were supposed to report and they would know what they were supposed to do more or less in that role. But there's no reason particularly why they should know the whole of it. In the fog of war, soldiers on the ground hardly ever, if at all, know what the big picture is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question refers to Defence Exhibit 55. I think we don't need it. It was a Defence Exhibit dealing with the renaming of units and headquarters of the Territorial Defence and the command and units of the army. Now, you have been a little bit cautious, I had the impression, with regard to the question of what was comprised by this renaming. Now, my question is: The village guards which have been established in some villages, have they ever become part of the army, of what it --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in the -- to the degree to which you noticed caution, I think I was trying to stress that all -- that in time of war, under the old defence doctrine, all the different elements become subordinated and part of one armed force. So there may be different elements of armed force, and this includes the MUP as well and any other paramilitary units, volunteer units, which includes also the volunteer guard units or civil defence, they all become part of one overall command structure. So when I was saying there's a specific law formally subjugating the Territorial Defence forces -- sorry, not subjugating, making them formally part of the designation of the army, and the Territorial Defence ceases to exist, I was trying to stress that, in fact, all armed forces were regarded as being part of this one whole armed force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But in an earlier statement you have been -- I mean, I asked you with regard to the village guards, you have been surprised, and you didn't really say very much about the character of the village guards. And we are -- that was my question, with regard to the two tiers.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Allow me --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the response and I don't recall the discussion either, I'm afraid. Are you able to help me on what the nature of the surprise might have been?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically the surprise was that you were not aware, actually, that there had been village --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of village guards. I was curious as to why there was significance attached to village guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. That was it, basically.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the overall system, you know, you would have people in villages guarding, both as volunteers, which I think was happening in this case, part of the process of getting volunteers, but also people with duties under the old civil protection or Territorial Defence systems as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My last question refers to your own book, "Triumph of the Lack of Will," which was turned in as Defence Exhibit D77. You speak of Muslim guerillas, Bosnian army corps units had conducted a series of raids in the area. Now, what do you mean by raid? "Raid" can be a rather broad expression.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't considered that it could have been a broad expression. I take it as being a fairly specific one. A raid is a mission, an operation, where forces go from one place to another, carry out an action, and then don't necessarily stay there and hold the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But what I'm --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: So a raiding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But what type of actions do they do during the raids.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, in these cases, they were reported as carrying out actions involving the use of firearms, munitions. The reports also say that places were burned, that there were allegations of massacres. Now, these are areas which, given what I understand about the nature of this case, I don't think it's my place to be talking about the detail on the ground, but as part of that overall strategic operational perspective, those raids were certainly taking place. They were taking place in terms of the guerilla strategy, about which I've said something, as a way of harassing the enemy and also building up strength, because one of the points in building an armed force is you're seeking to acquire strength. In some cases, capture weaponry and munitions. But recognising that if you sought to hold the territory once you'd raided, that you would probably lose it very soon. And indeed, where any territory was expanded and held in this particular part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, indeed, what happened once Serbian forces were concentrated there again. And the other aim was diversionary, as I pointed out this morning, coordinating actions so that a larger force could carry out a strategically more important operation, but as part of that strategic approach, seeking to kind of use up Serbian forces as far as possible, to give them two things to do at once rather than one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So the term raid may be clear, but what is done during a raid may be very different things.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's done -- yes, raid -- it's very simply -- is referring to a mission, an operation which has limited -- so an air raid, the aircraft, they take off from one place, they go, they carry out bombing or whatever, rocket, whatever, ground assault, on a particular place, and then they go back. Special forces carry out raiding missions. They'll go from one place, they'll go and carry out the operation. Then they'll return. The aim is not to stay there and to hold the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Brydensholt has a further question, and then I'll come to my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: We have seen that there were regulations for payment of some wages to soldiers, commanders, and so on, also to members of the Territorial Defence when they were actually participating in fighting. But you also added that even if those regulations were in place, that, as far as I remember you said, they were not always paid. You were aware of that. Could you elaborate a bit on that? Because that is of substance in this case here.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's simply that, although the personnel at times were owed monies, the money was not necessarily there to pay them and was not being used to pay them. That can happen to people in other walks of life as well, that they are contracted to be paid a certain amount, but the person responsible for paying it is not in a position to do it, or chooses not to do it because they don't have the money elsewhere. So I think there were reports, at times, that people in the VRS were not being paid. I wouldn't regard that necessarily -- I don't want to prejudge what's in Your Honour's mind. I wouldn't necessarily regard that as being a significant issue, whether or not they were actually paid. They were owed the money and promised that it would eventually be paid. But it is significant that when there were -- there was payment to officers, it came from Belgrade, and that when payment was passed down, presumably it was coming from -- to the lower ranks, it was presumably from the same budget as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Have you any idea how widespread the payment or non-payment was at all? Were they at all paid.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe people were paid, but intermittently. Whether or not anybody was ever paid all that they were owed, I'm afraid I don't know. And the extent is -- would be very hard to judge without going to find out specific information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I thought it could be that you have some documentation, but you don't.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I have a few questions. Monday you mentioned the Patriotic Front.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Patriotic League. Was it still in existence in the period, June 1992 till March 1993, or had it been integrated, as you've entered, within the -- either the territorial force or the army itself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've asked me a very good question to which I can't give a complete answer, because I don't actually know when, if at all, the Patriotic League ceased to exist. I do know that in that period, in April -- from April 1992 onwards, the Patriotic League was integrated into the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to General Sefer Halilovic, who was a member of the Patriotic League and who became part of it, and was then Chief of Staff in the Bosnian army. The Patriotic League was the spinal cord. This was the equivalent of the security service line that Milosevic's people had running through the JNA and into the VRS, VJ. It was something of that kind. It was the thing which provided the unifying element, the ghost in the machine of what became the Bosnian army. That's where the leading elements came from and where part of the defence planning prior to the formation of the army came from. I have to say, I don't actually know. It's a good question for me to go and find out when, if at all, it actually ended. And if Your Honour knows the answer, I would be very grateful to know as well. But what I do know is that it was integrated as part of the integration into the Bosnian army. Whether or not the Patriotic League and membership of it continued beyond the summer of 1992 or the autumn of 1992, I'm not certain. I've seen some Patriotic League membership cards. If I can find copies of them again, I'll go and see what dates they have on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did it have -- did the Patriotic League have a command structure? Was it based on -- did it have a command structure? And was it also divided by regions and by municipalities, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was initially and primarily a political organisation/body for purposes of preparing for defence. It had membership outside Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as inside it, within emigre, migrant communities. And within that political structure, the idea was to recruit people, who in some cases, in particular places, who would be the local people. I wouldn't go as far necessarily as to equate this with the crisis headquarters as part of the SDS campaign. But I see it as something going in the same direction. So it has a structure relating to the leadership of the SDA, Izetbegovic's Muslim-dominated party, and with a structure which then relates from that central leadership through a limited hierarchy to people in different places who will be in positions to assist or to take control when the time comes. Those people then, or significant numbers, are recruited into -- recruited into or integrated into the Bosnian army. But there's also a period in which the Patriotic League and, indeed, some other Muslim paramilitary forces are operating. The Patriotic League are the owners of the title Green Berets, which if you read around you will find references to. But the term is used loosely to refer to some of those other groups as well. But they are all groups which, as this evolution of the Bosnian army takes place, are formed into one. But in relation to an organisational structure which was in place to have them ready to be able to carry out missions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was there a parallel move or measure also taken on the Serbian side? In other words, were paramilitaries, for example, officially incorporated into the army, the Territorial Defence units? Were they officially incorporated into the army? Was this something which was the normality, in other words, as one went --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that -- my recollection is that I said something about this already, and that was that the paramilitaries on the Serbian side, which were primarily organised and coordinated by the Belgrade authorities, under a law of 1991, formally were treated as part of the Belgrade armed forces. I would assume -- and that was one integrated structure with the VRS, although formally separated for the purposes we discussed. And in that context, the paramilitary forces on the Serbian side, run by the Serbian security service, would be put under the command of the Yugoslav army, and the VRS would then be an extension of that. And if any units were operating, including the volunteer forces -- I mean, there were some volunteer forces raised and mobilised in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were put under the control of the VRS, which again was still part of the overall -- under the control of the VJ staff in Belgrade. So I think if that helps the answer, it's that it wasn't an exact parallel, but you have the Serbian security service in terms of planning paramilitary structures, political-military arrangements. That's, in some way, an equivalent to the Patriotic League, but it's not a precise equivalent. But they can form party organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, my intention was to draw a difference, if there is one. The next question is: Is there an official date that you could indicate for the coming into existence, officially, of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, it's the 15th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Halilovic, Sefer Halilovic, became Chief of Staff immediately.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think he was the second chief of -- I have to go back. There was briefly -- there was a brief period where there was another chief of staff, as I recall. If you bear with me, I can go back the dates in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not that important. I, again, like Judge Eser, am going to refer you to your own book, page -- could the witness please be given D77. In the meantime, I'm going to start reading. And the purpose of my reading this excerpt from your book is precisely because you use the word "crushing" yourself.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you seem to be using it as indicating a further escalation rather than a description of what had been ongoing. Please refer to the last paragraph on page 141, and then to -- as it continues on page 142: "The notion of safe areas first arose specifically over Srebrenica where the small, predominantly Muslim town in Eastern Bosnia had become the focal point of a Serbian campaign to drive Muslims out of the Drina valley, and where around 40.000 refugees from other communities in the region had fled. Eastern Bosnia had been swept by ethnic cleansing campaigns in the first month of the war in 1992, at which time numerous villages in that part of the country appear to be been razed. In the winter, conditions of January and February, Muslim guerillas and Bosnian army 2 Corps units had conducted a series of raids in the area, capturing territory from the Serbs and putting pressure on the Serbs at Bratunac, on the border between Bosnia and Serbia. In these attacks, there seemed to have been reprisal atrocities, meaning at a minimum summary executions. The Serb response to these operations and to the pressure on Bratunac and the Serbian border, and needing to secure territory to frustrate the Vance-Owen plan which they were coming under pressure to accept, was to begin a crushing campaign to eliminate remaining Muslim communities crush in Eastern Bosnia." I have two questions for you. How would you compare this crushing campaign that you mention at the end of this paragraph to what had been taking place earlier by the Serbs? And my second question to you is with regard to the raids that you mentioned. You maintain that these were being put -- made by Muslim guerillas and Bosnian army 2 Corps. Yesterday, or earlier on today, when you referred to these raids, and not in the context of what you have here, you mentioned also -- you passed the comment to Madam Vidovic, saying that, your client also was mentioned in the same context of many of these raids. If he was, as far as you are aware, would you place him amongst the Muslim guerillas, or would you place him within the Bosnian army 2 Corps? That's my question. Let's start with the last one. In this paragraph, did you mean to distinguish between the intensity of the ethnic cleansing campaign, as you describe it in the first part of the paragraph, and the crushing campaign to eliminate the remaining Muslim communities in Eastern Bosnia, as you refer to it in the last part of that paragraph? Or is it just that I am being carried away with my imagination.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have to do at least two things here. The first is to separate out the beginning of the paragraph from the end. The beginning of the paragraph is referring generally to Eastern Bosnia and the manner in which the campaign of ethnic cleansing had resulted in a situation where most of Eastern Bosnia had been depopulated of Muslims, and that many of those Muslims, several tens of thousands of them, had ended up in the places -- in the enclaves, in Srebrenica, Zepa, and in Gorazde. So the first part is referring to the initial campaign in the spring and summer of 1992, a situation which left Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, as enclaves still with Muslim populations, including those who'd fled there from other places. The second part of it and the reference to crushing campaign, you're quite right in your initial comment to identify a sense of intensification, but not a sense of intensification necessarily from the first part of the paragraph, but from the situation immediately preceding. You made reference to the testimony earlier regarding the 2 Corps operations and the use of the guerilla operations vis-a-vis that strategically. Bosnian Serb forces, because control of the Posavina Corridor had been broken in December/January on two occasions, the VRS and VJ reinforcements had concentrated, first of all, on securing control of the corridor. So this whole area had been relatively quiet in Serbian terms and had not been used significantly -- significant Serbian forces had not been there during this period. The Serbian forces was relatively weak in the area, one of the reasons why the area under control could be expanded in some of this time. But once the corridor had been secured again, some of those forces were moved around in Serbia, and the VJ forces were then used to concentrate on trying to eliminate this enclave, and of course with it, the resistance which had been shown to the Serbian campaign and the project and the degree to which that had been able to have been successful in widening the territory of the enclave. So the crushing is about the intensification, and the very strong and heavy intensification, and I think that was represented in the UNPROFOR report that I was shown by Madam Vidovic before the break, where the UN military personnel and the EC monitors in the area were reporting quite how intense the Serbian campaign had become. So the crushing there is an adjective intensifying the campaign at that point, in that place. And I would still, going back to the question of "crush" earlier on, I would point out that I was simply making -- the crush in that context as a verb could have physical implications which were not consistent with what was in the original language, text of the document at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the other point, the accused, whether you would fit him under the Bosnian army 2 Corps or the Muslim guerillas, since you had heard that it was sort of -- the way I understood you was that news about these raids included also a mention of the accused's name. So in which of these two contexts? Or just in regard to raids generally.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think initially there can be no doubt that the accused's name appeared in relation to the emergence of this guerilla force operating in Eastern Bosnia, and its relative success. That goes back even to the initial takeover -- attempted takeover by the Serbian forces. They entered Srebrenica on the 18th of April. As I understand it, even by the 20th, the accused was involved in leading, initially, raiding missions which then became more successful, but because the Serbian forces thought initially on the 18th they dealt with Srebrenica and didn't have it under full control. It eventually led to a situation in which Srebrenica, the enclave, emerged. So the initial association is in leading those raids on a guerilla basis at that stage, and that's a reputation which, I think, grows in the course of 1992, in the situation in Srebrenica, and particularly in late 1992 when the operations appear to have been, in Bosnian terms, more and more successful. By the time we come to the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, that association and the understanding that the accused is still leading those operations has to be put in the context that the formal army of Bosnia-Herzegovina has been informed that a structure has been put in place formally, that the implementation of that structure has been taking place, that the 2 Corps exists and covers Eastern Bosnia, these parts of Eastern Bosnia, and that any forces operating should be regarded as, again, in line with all the things we've said about defence doctrine and things like that, as having been under the authority of 2 Corps and indeed, as part of it. But they were still operating, they were still physically cut off from the remainder of 2 Corps, but there were connections and coordination about the use of these raiding missions in December/January to divert attention, to draw off Serbian forces as far as possible, to allow the concentration on the Posavina Corridor. So I would see it at that stage of being certainly -- probably at any stage from August formally and technically as being part of 2 Corps, whatever it was, or under the authority of 2 Corps. But certainly at that stage was involved as part of 2 Corps operations, but still having this distinctive guerilla character and operating in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My last questions. Are you aware of an attack on the village of Ratkovici between the 21st and the 27th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of an attack on the village of Jezestica and the hamlet of Bozici on the 8th of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware, at least not as such. I may well have read about these things but I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with these places, Ratkovici, Jezestica, Fakovici, Jelovac.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the name Jezestica. But, I mean, Ratkovici is a name I've heard, but then I cannot -- I have to say also that many of these names crop up so many times in different places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, are you familiar with an alleged attack, the Prosecution is alleging that the accused led an attack on the 5th of October, 1992, on the village of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not specifically familiar with that. I have to say, if these are -- if all of the names are in the indictment, and I was given a copy of the indictment to read. But I've never regarded it as being my business to go to the detail of the cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure whether you are aware of these facts --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- not through reading the indictment.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the point I want to make.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say I would be aware through that. I think it's quite likely I would be aware of them through reading, for example, my colleague's book, Dr. Hornig's book on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again, the attack on village of Bjelovac between the 14th and the 19th of December, and the joining hamlet of Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're going to get the same answer to all of these questions, which is that I will have read about these sorts of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, so you were --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I have no specific knowledge about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are not in the position to confirm to us that the alleged attacks on these villages, if, indeed, they did take place, were part of this diversion --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, no, I can help you on that count, because the dates you gave were not part of the -- were prior to the diversionary action. The diversionary action was the end of 1992. You read out dates in May and June, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The dates are June, August, October, December, and then January of 1993 and January of --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW JAMES WILLIAM GOW [Resumed]
utterances.text: December and January operations could -- probably should be seen as part of the diversionary effort, the diversionary effort was also -- also had the complementary guerilla, local issues attached to it as well, securing control of territory, if possible. But certainly December/January would be part of the -- as well as being operations in the area, but it would also be part of the diversionary campaign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I don't think we have any further questions, which basically means, Dr. Gow, that your testimony comes to an end here. I thank you for your -- first of all, for accepting to be an expert witness in this case, and for coming over and spending basically three days with us. And I thank you on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, but I also thank you on behalf of the Tribunal. You will be escorted now out of the courtroom by Mr. Usher, and I'm sure you will receive all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, evacuation. On behalf of everyone present here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much to Your Honour, and thank you to Your Honours for conducting this in such a pleasant manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose there is nothing else, no further business to transact today, which is perfectly convenient for me. I go to bed now and try to get rid of this cold that I have, which is becoming worse and not better. Tomorrow morning, we have the videolink; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I wish -- I'm sure that you will do your best to finish it tomorrow, because otherwise we will have problems. On Friday, we will have Manas testifying, and then we will deal with those matters that I mentioned on Monday, the outstanding motions, okay? I thank you so much. The sitting is adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9. We start at 9, just the same, for the videolink, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's up to the Registry. You instructed the Registry to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The instructions are for 9.00, but I don't know if -- all right, okay. Everything is in place. Thank you so much. We will be here in this courtroom, no? Or courtroom 3, I think. Courtroom 3 we're going to be tomorrow. Okay. We will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be resumed on Thursday, 25 November 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.15 p.m.,
